title: “We kept the wrong measurement”: an interview with the field team
intro: Four questions about instruments, trust and the week the calibration drifted.

add_image.image_alt: Two researchers talking beside an instrument case
add_image.image_caption: Carlos Mendoza and Min-jun Park, after the morning calibration.
add_image.content_to_show_on_side_of_the_image_whe: The interview took place at the station bench, between the 07:00 calibration and the first run of the day. The recorder was left running while the instruments warmed up.

add_heading.heading_text: The first sign something was wrong

add_quote.text: The numbers were plausible. That is the dangerous part — a wrong measurement that looks right will survive three weeks of review.

add_content_to_page.add_paragraph: The discrepancy started at 3% and grew. It was easy to attribute to weather, then to a tired sensor, then to the reference itself. Each explanation bought another day.
A shade, a longer equilibration time and a temperature log. None of it was clever. All of it was cheap. The expensive part was admitting that the first week could not be used.

add_quote.text: We did not lose a week of data. We learned what the first week was actually measuring.

add_items_to_list: Log the environment, not just the measurand.
Calibrate against a reference that shares the same conditions.
Write down the moment you stop trusting a series — with the time.
Keep the raw files, even when you know you will not use them.
